In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

in young hypertensive patients, the active postural changes in ANP levels, in the presence or in the absence of positive family background, are similar to those observed in young normotensive subjects.

in the presence of an active postural inhibition, the circulating ANP levels are similar in young normotensives, in young normotensive subjects from a family history of hypertension and in young hypertensive patients.
in hypertensive patients, as in normotensive subjects, ANP release is actively inhibited by postural changes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the orthostatic inhibition of ANP is not related to hypertension, nor to the presence of hypertensive parents.
the ANP system does not seem to be involved in the pathogenesis of hypertension in the young, at least in the early stages of the disease.
, in young hypertensive patients, the ANP release is not impaired and the ANP levels do not increase after a 60 min period of recumbency.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ANP response to the orthostatic test was not different in young hypertensive patients and in normotensive subjects, regardless of their family history of hypertension.
ANP release is reduced in response to orthostatic challenge.
the active posturocardiac regulation is not impaired in young hypertensive patients, even if a positive family history of hypertension is present.
